claims.text: The strength–ductility balance of dynamically loaded Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by deformation twinning via stacking-fault formation supplementing dislocation slip.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates enhance twin nucleation in FeNiCrMn.
Enhanced twin nucleation provides additional strain hardening that compensates for constrained dislocation slip.
The proposed initial material is solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn with a homogeneous microstructure and minimal pre-existing defects.
Temperature and strain rate will be varied during in situ tensile and compression testing in a TEM.
The proposed study spans approximately -100 °C to 200 °C and strain rates of about 10^-4 to 10^3 s^-1.
Dynamic deformation is mediated by the interplay between dislocation slip and stacking-fault-driven twin formation.
At lower temperatures and elevated strain rates, increased lattice resistance promotes local stacking-fault formation.
Local stacking faults trigger the nucleation and growth of deformation twins.
Deformation twins impede dislocation motion and thereby enhance strain hardening without sacrificing ductility.
At higher temperatures or lower strain rates, deformation is accommodated predominantly by dislocation slip.
High-strain-rate, low-temperature loading will produce increased twin density and more stacking-fault features.
Increased twin density and stacking-fault activity will correlate with enhanced strain hardening.
Less extreme temperature and strain-rate conditions will show lower twin density and predominantly dislocation-mediated deformation.
Under quasi-static loading at room temperature, dislocation slip is the primary deformation mechanism and twinning is minimal.
The proposed mechanism applies between -100 °C and 200 °C and between approximately 10^-4 and 10^3 s^-1.
Conditions outside the stated window may activate additional deformation modes.
Failure to observe an increase in twin density under low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading relative to baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a correlation between strain hardening and twin or stacking-fault formation would falsify the hypothesis.
